title: The long story of a past Buddha (Kern ch. 7)
word: The long story of a past Buddha
hook: a Buddha of ages past and his sixteen sons who taught

segments.voice: Yesterday, vyakarana: the great disciples, like starving men at a royal meal, heard the Buddha name each one's future. Your line: a future foretold. Did you tell someone to go ahead? Day one thousand one hundred sixty.

Yesterday looked forward, into futures. Chapter seven of the Lotus turns all the way around and looks back, so far back that the sutra needs a whole picture just to say how long ago. The Diamond Sutra ground a world to dust to ask what a heap is. The Lotus grinds a world to dust to measure time. Carry the dust across the worlds, and let fall one speck only after crossing a great stretch of them, until the dust is gone. The time since this story is longer than that. Then the Buddha begins, the way old stories do. Today: the long story of a past Buddha.
screen: `FROM FUTURES TO THE PAST.` → `DUST THAT MEASURES TIME.` → `LONGER AGO THAN THAT.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha of long ago. Kern gives his name as Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu, a long name to say even once. He sat at the seat of awakening, and for a long time the full awakening did not come. He stayed seated, steady, until at last it did. Second, the sons. Before he left home, the story says, this Buddha had been a prince with sixteen sons. When they heard their father had awakened, they left their toys and their palaces and went to honor him, with their family following behind. They asked him to teach. Kings of the heavens came too, from every direction, offering their palaces and asking the same thing. Third, the sons as teachers. Their father taught the early teachings first, and many were freed. Later, the sixteen sons, now young monks, asked him for more, and he taught them this very sutra, the Lotus. Then he went into a long meditation. While he sat, each of the sixteen sons took a seat and taught the Lotus to the crowds, in detail, for a long time. Fourth, where they are now. Here is the turn. Those sixteen sons, the Buddha says, are all Buddhas now, teaching in different directions. One of them, in the west, is called Amitayus. And the sixteenth son, he says, is me. I am the one who taught you then. The listeners in front of him today, the sutra says, are the same beings he taught as that young monk, ages ago. The long story isn't a detour. It tells the disciples why they are here. The teaching they are hearing has a lineage older than they can picture, passed from father to sons, from sons to listeners, and they were already in it. That's why yesterday's promises were not new. They were old seeds coming up.
screen: `A BUDDHA OF AGES PAST.` · `A PRINCE WITH SIXTEEN SONS.` · `THE SONS TEACH THE LOTUS.` · `THE SIXTEENTH SON IS ME.` · then, large: `SIXTEEN SONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: honor an old lineage. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of something you know how to do, a craft, a song, a recipe, a way of praying or sitting, and ask who taught it to you. Then ask who taught them. Follow the chain back as far as you can, face by face, until the faces blur. Rest there, at the edge of what you can see, and simply be grateful to everyone in the line, known and unknown. The bell holds the time.
The long story of a past Buddha. In chapter seven, a Buddha of ages past teaches the Lotus to his sixteen sons, who teach it in turn; the sixteenth is the Buddha who tells the story. Today's word.
screen: `THE LONG STORY OF A PAST BUDDHA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sixteen sons. Today, thank one person in your own chain of teachers, living or not, out loud or in a quiet word. Day one thousand one hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Some Lotus Sutra readers in East Asia study chapter seven's story of the ancient Buddha and his sixteen sons as the account of the Buddha's long bond with his hearers; some readers link the mention of Amitayus in the west to Pure Land devotion.

original.note: Sanskrit: former connection, ancient bond; the name of chapter seven in Kern's Sanskrit text.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long, old fairy tale.
what it means: the teaching has passed down an ancient line, from a past Buddha to his sons to the listeners now.
what a scholar hears: purvayoga, the former bond, explains the chapter six predictions: the hearers were taught by the Buddha as the sixteenth son long ago.

notes: Chapter 7 paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884); nothing quoted.

Check: the dust-of-a-world image for the length of time (Kern gives specific counts, omitted); the name Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu as Kern spells it; the delay before full awakening (Kern gives a number of intermediate ages, omitted); the sons' family following them (Kumarajiva has mothers and the grandfather-king; simplified to 'their family'); the Brahma kings from the directions; the sixteen sons as novices teaching while their father was in meditation; Amitayus/Amitabha in the west and Shakyamuni as the sixteenth.
The phrase 'old seeds coming up' is an image, not a quoted term.
Original: Purvayoga (पूर्वयोग); Kern renders the chapter title along the lines of 'ancient devotion'; check.
